nameStory: The straight-lanced meadow katydid gets its name from the remarkably straight, lance-like shape of its wings when viewed from above. Unlike many of its meadow katydid cousins that have curved or angled wing edges, this species sports wings that taper in nearly perfect straight lines from base to tip, like a medieval knight's lance.
description: The straight-lanced meadow katydid is a slender, green grasshopper-like insect that's actually more closely related to crickets than true grasshoppers. These delicate insects have long, thread-like antennae that can be twice as long as their body, and narrow wings that extend well beyond their abdomen. Adults typically measure about an inch long, with a streamlined build that helps them navigate through tall grasses and meadow plants where they spend their lives.

idTips.label: Wing shape
idTips.description: Wings have distinctly straight outer edges that taper evenly from base to tip, creating a lance-like appearance when viewed from above - no curves or bends

idTips.label: Body color
idTips.description: Bright green overall with a pale yellowish or whitish stripe running down the back, sometimes with subtle brown markings on the head

idTips.label: Antennae length
idTips.description: Extremely long, thin antennae that feel delicate to the touch and are often twice the body length - much longer than a grasshopper's stubby antennae

idTips.label: Wing length
idTips.description: Wings extend well past the tip of the abdomen, often by a third of the body length or more, giving a streamlined silhouette

idTips.label: Sound production
idTips.description: Males produce a continuous, high-pitched buzzing or ticking sound by rubbing their wings together - softer and more musical than grasshopper chirps

habitat: Look for straight-lanced meadow katydids in wet meadows, marsh edges, and grassy areas near streams or ponds throughout New England. They prefer tall, dense grasses and sedges where they can climb and hide, often found in the same areas where red-winged blackbirds nest. These katydids thrive in moderately wet soils and are common in both coastal and inland wetland margins.

seasonality.spring: Adults are not yet present. Look for tiny, wingless nymphs in late spring that resemble miniature green grasshoppers with oversized antennae.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity time when adults emerge and begin singing. Males are most vocal during warm evenings, producing their characteristic buzzing calls from perches on grass stems.
seasonality.fall: Adults remain active through early fall, continuing to sing and mate. This is often the easiest time to spot them as vegetation begins to thin and their green color stands out more.
seasonality.winter: Adults die with the first hard frosts. Eggs overwinter in plant stems or soil, completely hidden from view until the following spring.

funFact: Male straight-lanced meadow katydids are acoustic perfectionists - they can adjust the pitch of their wing-chirping in real-time to match the temperature, producing higher notes on warm nights and lower tones when it's cool, like a living thermometer you can hear!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other meadow katydids in the same genus, but the straight wing edges are the giveaway - if the wing edges are curved, notched, or wavy, it's a different species. Remember: 'Straight-lanced = straight wings' - the name tells you exactly what to look for.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called katydids, meadow katydids like this species don't actually say 'katy-did' - that's the sound made by their larger, broad-winged cousins. The meadow katydids produce more subtle buzzing or ticking sounds, leading to some confusion when people expect to hear the classic 'katy-did' call.
compareHints: Among New England's meadow katydids, the straight-lanced stands out for its perfectly straight wing edges - the short-winged has wings that don't extend past its body, the slender has curved wing edges, and the saltmarsh is found only in coastal salt marshes. If you see long wings with ruler-straight edges in a freshwater wetland, you've found the straight-lanced species.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its meadow katydid relatives, the short-winged species is immediately recognizable by its abbreviated wings - all other Conocephalus species in New England have long wings that extend to or beyond the tip of their abdomen.
Among New England's meadow katydids, the slender meadow katydid lives up to its name with the thinnest, most elongated body of the group.

Unlike the Short-winged Meadow Katydid which has reduced wings and prefers wet meadows, or the Slender Meadow Katydid found in freshwater marshes, the Saltmarsh Meadow Katydid is distinguished by its exclusive salt marsh habitat and well-developed wings.
